pfc.title: Keep the rule
pfc.idea: Helps you keep a goal in mind and ignore distractions.
pfc.invite: Can you hold a rule while something else tries to grab your attention?
pfc.instruction: Remember the rule, wait through the distraction, then choose the matching card.
why: You need to keep the rule available while the original instruction is out of sight.
A distracting card competes for attention. Keeping the goal and selecting a response involve prefrontal interactions with other networks.
Your answer is a task response, not a measurement of your prefrontal activity.
pfc.try_next: Try the same rule with no distraction, then add distraction. Change one setting at a time.
pfc.depth: Delay-related activity in some prefrontal neurons supports studying how goals remain available. Recurrent excitation, inhibition and synaptic dynamics can contribute; no single cell is the whole plan.
pfc.scope: A short human task; no brain activity or cognitive capacity is measured.

occipital.title: Find the edge
occipital.idea: Helps turn visual input into useful features such as edges and orientation.
occipital.invite: Make a drawing and see which simple visual filter responds.
occipital.instruction: Click the pixels. Compare a vertical edge, a horizontal edge and a uniform patch.
why: Each filter combines nearby bright and dark pixels differently.
Changing an edge's orientation changes which filter responds most. A uniform bright patch can give a smaller edge response than a boundary.
These are hand-set filters, not a simulation of a retina or a learned visual cortex.
occipital.try_next: Keep the pixels fixed and lower contrast. Does the preferred orientation change, or just the response size?
occipital.depth: Real V1 populations have receptive fields and orientation selectivity shaped by many interacting inputs. Retinal, thalamic, local cortical and feedback processing precede or contribute to visual interpretation.
occipital.scope: A simplified feature-filter model; it does not recognise arbitrary objects.

cerebellum.title: Adjust the reach
cerebellum.idea: Helps fine-tune actions when the result differs from what was expected.
cerebellum.invite: The cursor has been shifted. Can repeated error help the model compensate?
cerebellum.instruction: Make a reach, repeat it, then remove the shift without resetting the learned compensation.
why: The visible error is the difference between the cursor endpoint and the target.
The model changes a compensating command after each reach. With learning enabled, the same shift produces less error over repeated trials.
Remove the shift: retained compensation can produce an error in the opposite direction, an aftereffect in this model.
cerebellum.try_next: Set learning to zero and repeat the same shift. Compare with a fresh run with learning enabled.
cerebellum.depth: Human reaching experiments connect cerebellar function with sensory prediction error and adaptation. Real mossy, parallel, climbing-fibre and Purkinje-cell circuits are much richer than this scalar update.
cerebellum.scope: An error-based adaptation analogy, not a Purkinje-cell or muscle simulation.

temporal.title: Recognise a changed shape
temporal.idea: Helps connect visual features with what an object is.
temporal.invite: Teach two different drawings, then test an edited version without giving the answer.
temporal.instruction: Edit Example 1 and Example 2 independently. Teach them, draw a test input, and ask the frozen circuit.
why: Teaching changes the circuit's readout weights using labelled examples.
The test sends only the drawn pixels and learned weights to the circuit. It does not send the expected class.
An edited input can change its response or make it undecided. Recognising taught shapes does not prove general object understanding.
temporal.try_next: Flip one test pixel without teaching again. Then try two pixels. Which change alters the response?
temporal.depth: Ventral visual pathways contribute object-related representations. The experiment uses a fixed spiking encoder and supervised readout, not the full temporal cortex or biologically learned visual invariance.
temporal.scope: Real 100-cell model outputs; the cell groups are engineering roles, not brain regions.

parietal.title: Move the spotlight
parietal.idea: Helps select locations and relate sensory information to action.
parietal.invite: The scene stays the same. Can moving attention change which location wins?
parietal.instruction: Click a location to move the model spotlight. Watch the selected location and weighted evidence.
why: Every location still has the same sensory input.
The spotlight changes the weight given to nearby locations. A previously losing location can become the strongest weighted signal.
Changing selection is different from deleting input. This is not a simulation of clinical neglect.
parietal.try_next: Set attention gain to zero. Does moving the spotlight still change the selected location?
parietal.depth: Posterior parietal and frontal networks participate in spatial selection and action-related transformations. A Gaussian gain field illustrates one computation, not their complete physiology.
parietal.scope: A spatial-weighting model with fixed input, not a diagnostic attention test.

hippocampus.title: Remember what went where
hippocampus.idea: Helps form links between an event, its place and its context.
hippocampus.invite: Link two cues with two places, then retrieve the place from the cue alone.
hippocampus.instruction: Give each editable cue a place. Teach the pair, then query a cue without supplying its place.
why: During teaching, a cue is paired with a place label. Later, the query contains only the cue pixels.
The receiving population's voltage chooses a learned response, which is then displayed as its taught place.
Change the place assignments and teach again to explore interference. This is a readout association, not episodic recollection or hippocampal pattern completion.
hippocampus.try_next: Swap the two places and teach again. Compare the same cue before and after the new association.
hippocampus.depth: Medial-temporal networks help form certain new memories. Dentate gyrus, CA3, CA1 and entorhinal pathways have distinct roles; this fixed-encoder readout does not reproduce those circuits.
hippocampus.scope: A cue–place learning analogy using the 100-cell circuit; no human memory is measured.

basal.title: Learn which action pays
basal.idea: Helps shape action selection through connected learning and control loops.
basal.invite: Try two actions. Change their outcomes and watch the model adapt its preference.
basal.instruction: Choose an action or let the model take a small batch of turns. Then reverse the outcomes.
why: Each chosen action has an expected outcome, shown by its learned value.
Only the chosen action is updated using outcome minus expectation. A surprising outcome changes that value more than an expected one.
Basal-ganglia learning includes dopamine-related and inhibitory circuit mechanisms. These two values are an abstract model, not dopamine concentrations.
basal.try_next: Reverse Action 1 and Action 2 outcomes while retaining learned values. Watch how earlier learning influences the next choices.
basal.depth: Cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loops combine excitation, inhibition and modulation. Direct/indirect pathway summaries help trace signs, but they are not a complete action-selection theory.
basal.scope: An action-value model; a preference is not a probability of human behaviour.

motor.title: Combine direction signals
motor.idea: Helps send movement-related commands through descending pathways.
motor.invite: Several direction-tuned model populations can combine into one movement vector.
motor.instruction: Choose a command direction. Reduce one population and compare the resulting movement arrow.
why: Each model population prefers a different direction.
Their weighted vectors add together. Reducing an active contributor can change the size and direction of the combined vector.
Real motor output also depends on muscles, spinal circuits, posture and feedback. A population vector is one useful model, not the whole motor code.
motor.try_next: Suppress a population near the command direction, then one facing away. Do both manipulations have the same effect?
motor.depth: Primate recordings motivated population-vector descriptions of directional activity. Individual cells and whole motor circuits also reflect variables beyond direction.
motor.scope: Eight idealised directional populations, not a muscle or corticospinal simulation.

thalamus.title: Let one signal through
thalamus.idea: Helps regulate information flow in connected relay circuits.
thalamus.invite: Two inputs arrive. Change the relay gains without changing those inputs.
thalamus.instruction: Set Channel 1 and Channel 2 independently. Open one route while reducing the other.
why: Input and transmission are separate variables.
The model relays input multiplied by gain, reduced by inhibition. Different outputs can therefore follow the same incoming signals.
Biological thalamic nuclei receive driving, modulating and inhibitory inputs. A gain slider does not calculate attention or thalamic burst currents.
thalamus.try_next: Keep both incoming strengths equal and swap only the gains. Which stage changed the outgoing evidence?
thalamus.depth: Visual LGN and reticular activity can be modulated during attention in macaque tasks. Thalamic processing also depends on membrane state and connected cortical/brainstem inputs.
thalamus.scope: An explicit gated-current analogy, not measured human attention.

amygdala.title: Give a cue a consequence
amygdala.idea: Helps connect learned significance with cues and responses.
amygdala.invite: A neutral cue predicts confetti. What happens when the expected event stops arriving?
amygdala.instruction: Pair a cue with an outcome, test it without teaching, then run unpaired presentations.
why: The cue appears before the model receives an outcome. The expectation is read before the update.
Repeated pairings change the cue's learned expectation. Presenting it with no outcome reduces that expectation in this simple rule.
Unlike action learning, no choice earns the outcome here. Confetti is neutral: the experiment does not simulate emotion or fear.
amygdala.try_next: Teach Cue 1, then probe it with no update. Next run no-outcome presentations. A frozen probe and new teaching answer different questions.
amygdala.depth: Amygdala conditioning research concerns interacting nuclei and distributed plasticity. Reduced expectation in this scalar model does not reproduce all mechanisms of biological extinction.
amygdala.scope: Neutral cue association; no emotion, fear response or amygdala activity is measured.

hypothalamus.title: Keep an internal balance
hypothalamus.idea: Helps coordinate responses to the body's internal needs.
hypothalamus.invite: Disturb an internal state and see how feedback helps bring it towards a target.
hypothalamus.instruction: Change the outside condition. Compare feedback ON and OFF while watching the same internal state.
why: The outside condition pushes the model's internal state away from its target.
Feedback uses the difference from the target to adjust warming or cooling. Turn feedback off to see what the disturbance does without that response.
The units are arbitrary. This does not calculate human temperature, hormones or medical regulation.
hypothalamus.try_next: After settling in a warm environment, make the outside cold. Does the controller need the same response?
hypothalamus.depth: Different hypothalamic populations integrate physiological information and influence autonomic, endocrine and behavioural pathways. This small feedback controller illustrates an organising principle rather than those exact pathways.
hypothalamus.scope: An artificial internal-state controller in model units, not body temperature.

brainstem.title: Generate a repeating rhythm
brainstem.idea: Contains circuits that support basic rhythms, state and communication pathways.
brainstem.invite: Can a small adapting unit generate repeated pulses without a new instruction each time?
brainstem.instruction: Run the rhythm, change its drive and recovery, then remove the drive.
why: Drive raises the model unit towards a firing threshold.
A pulse resets it and increases a temporary brake. As that brake recovers, another pulse becomes possible.
Real brainstem rhythms involve specialised interacting populations and feedback. These pulses are not a breathing prescription or a complete respiratory model.
brainstem.try_next: Keep recovery fixed and reduce drive to zero. Then restore drive. Which component initiates the next pulse?
brainstem.depth: Medullary and pontine respiratory networks combine excitatory, inhibitory and modulatory influences. Sleep/wake and cranial pathways involve other connected nuclei, not one universal rhythm cell.
brainstem.scope: An adapting threshold-unit analogy in arbitrary time units, not human breathing.
